name: Aortic valve
func: A three-cusp one-way valve at the exit of the left ventricle. It opens to let the ventricle pump blood into the aorta and snaps shut afterward so blood can't fall back into the heart.

levels.kid:
When the strongest room of your heart, the left ventricle, squeezes, blood has to leave through a special door to get into the body's biggest tube, the aorta. That door is the **aortic valve**.

It has three little cup-shaped flaps. When blood rushes out, the cups fold flat against the wall. When the push is over, blood tries to fall back, fills the three cups, and they puff up and touch, closing the door tight.

That closing makes the "dub" part of your heartbeat's "lub-dub." Right next to the door are two tiny openings that feed blood to the heart muscle itself.
levels.hs:
The **aortic valve** guards the exit from the **left ventricle** into the **aorta**. It is a **semilunar valve** (half-moon shaped) with three **cusps**: the **right coronary**, **left coronary** and **non-coronary** cusps. It sits in the center of the heart, wedged between the mitral valve (behind and to its left), the pulmonary valve (in front and to its left) and the tricuspid valve (to its right), behind the left half of the sternum at about the third intercostal space.

Unlike the atrioventricular valves, it has **no chordae or papillary muscles**. It closes passively when blood falls back and fills its cusps.

Just above each cusp the aortic wall bulges into a pocket called an **aortic sinus (sinus of Valsalva)**. The **right and left coronary arteries** start from the right and left sinuses, so the heart feeds itself first.

Its closure, with the pulmonary valve's, makes the **second heart sound (S2)**. Doctors listen best at the **right upper sternal border** (2nd intercostal space). About 1–2% of people are born with a **bicuspid aortic valve** (two cusps), the most common congenital heart defect.
levels.college:
The aortic root includes the **annulus**, the cusps, the **interleaflet triangles**, the three **sinuses of Valsalva** and the **sinotubular junction** where the root meets the tubular ascending aorta. The cusps hinge along a crown-shaped (semilunar) line, not a flat ring, so "annulus" is a surgical and imaging convention measured at the cusps' lowest points.

Each cusp has a thickened central nodule (**nodule of Arantius**) and thin edges (**lunulae**) that overlap during closure to seal the orifice.

Relations: the non-coronary and left cusps sit above the **anterior mitral leaflet** (fibrous continuity). The membranous septum, and the **bundle of His** running beneath it, sit just under the junction of the right and non-coronary cusps, explaining why valve calcification, endocarditis abscesses and transcatheter valves can cause **heart block**.

Normal valve area is about 3–4 cm²; severe **aortic stenosis** is usually defined as under 1.0 cm², a mean gradient of 40 mmHg or more, or a peak velocity of 4 m/s or more on Doppler.

The coronaries fill mainly during **diastole**, when the valve is closed and the myocardium is relaxed. That's why problems that lower diastolic aortic pressure, such as aortic regurgitation, can starve the heart muscle.
levels.phd:
**Calcific aortic valve disease (CAVD)**, the main cause of stenosis in older adults, was once seen as passive "wear and tear" but is an active, atherosclerosis-like process. It starts on the **aortic (fibrosa) side** of the cusp, where disturbed, low and oscillating shear stress activates the endothelium. **Lipoprotein(a)** and oxidized LDL infiltrate, macrophages and T cells follow, and **valvular interstitial cells** differentiate toward an **osteoblast-like phenotype** (RUNX2, BMP2, Wnt/β-catenin signaling), laying down hydroxyapatite and sometimes true lamellar bone.

Genome-wide studies identified **LPA** (lipoprotein(a)) as a strong causal locus. Interestingly, statins, which slow atherosclerosis, failed to slow established CAVD in trials, suggesting calcification becomes self-sustaining once mineralization begins. Lp(a)-lowering therapies are now being tested.

The **bicuspid aortic valve** usually arises from fusion of the right and left coronary cusps. It is associated with mutations in **NOTCH1** and **GATA** family genes and with an **aortopathy**: the ascending aorta dilates even independent of flow disturbance, due to abnormal neural crest–derived smooth muscle and matrix. Bicuspid valves calcify decades earlier than tricuspid ones.

In severe stenosis, the LV responds with **concentric hypertrophy**; the thickened muscle outgrows its microcirculation, causing subendocardial ischemia and fibrosis that may not fully reverse after valve replacement.
levels.expert:
**Aortic stenosis (AS)** gives a **harsh ejection systolic (crescendo–decrescendo) murmur** at the right upper sternal border radiating to the **carotids**, a **slow-rising, low-volume pulse** (**pulsus parvus et tardus**) and a soft or absent S2. The classic symptom triad is **angina, syncope and heart failure**; once symptoms appear, prognosis without treatment is poor.

**Aortic regurgitation (AR)** gives an **early diastolic decrescendo murmur** at the left sternal border (best heard sitting forward, breath held in expiration), a **wide pulse pressure** and a **collapsing (water-hammer) pulse**. Eponymous signs include **de Musset's** (head bobbing), **Quincke's** (nail-bed pulsation) and **Corrigan's** (visible carotid pulsation).

Neurological links: **calcific emboli** from a degenerated valve, endocarditis vegetations causing stroke or **mycotic aneurysms**, and periprocedural stroke after valve replacement, often silent on MRI. Bicuspid valves are associated with **coarctation of the aorta**, which itself carries an increased rate of **intracranial (berry) aneurysms**.

Imaging: echo grades severity; **CT** sizes the annulus and plans transcatheter access; calcium scoring helps when echo is ambiguous.

Treatment in general terms: there is no drug that reverses stenosis. Severe symptomatic AS is treated by **surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR)** or **transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI/TAVR)**, the latter delivered usually through the femoral artery. Complications of TAVI include stroke, heart block needing a pacemaker, and leaks around the valve.

keyPoints: Exit valve of the left ventricle into the aorta; three cusps
Coronary arteries arise from the sinuses just above it
Closure contributes to S2; heard best at the right upper sternal border
AS: ejection murmur to carotids; triad angina, syncope, heart failure
Bicuspid valve: most common congenital heart defect

test.q: Which cusp of the aortic valve has NO coronary artery arising above it?
test.explain: The right and left coronary arteries arise from the right and left sinuses; the third is the non-coronary cusp.

test.q: Where does the murmur of aortic stenosis classically radiate?
test.explain: AS murmur radiates along the direction of flow up into the carotids.

test.q: Pouches of the aortic wall just above each cusp are called the sinuses of ______.
test.explain: The sinuses of Valsalva house the coronary ostia and help the cusps close smoothly.

test.q: The classic symptom triad of severe aortic stenosis is:
test.explain: Fixed outflow obstruction causes ischemia (angina), poor brain perfusion on exertion (syncope) and failure.

test.q: A congenital aortic valve with two cusps is called a ______ aortic valve.
test.explain: Present in about 1–2% of people; it calcifies early and is linked to aortic dilation and coarctation.
